output.title: Maintenance windows are a workflow choice, not just a calendar slot
output.body:
If you run a small business, rethinking maintenance windows usually comes down to one recurring decision: do you bundle changes into planned downtime, spread them out as rolling updates, or use a hybrid? The useful question is not which sounds modern. It is which one costs you less in practice: planned customer-visible outage or unplanned breakdowns.

For a 1–10 person team, the right answer often depends on whether the work is already repeatable. If you have a standard pre-maintenance message, a checklist, a rollback step, and a log of what changed, that is a sign the workflow may be worth tightening. In that case, automation can help with sequencing, reminders, and record-keeping. It should not make the go/no-go call for you. Human approval still belongs at the point where service might be interrupted or risk increases.

That is the kind of boundary we look for in a diagnostic: one recurring workflow, one decision owner, one clear outcome. If the maintenance process is mostly email, notes, and tool-jumping, the next step is to map the handoffs before trying to automate anything. Otherwise you risk building a tidy machine around a messy habit. Clever, but not useful.

Bareni treats this as a bounded workflow question, not a promise that AI belongs everywhere. Some maintenance setups are a fit for a small pilot; others are better left manual. The useful part is finding that line before you spend time on the wrong side of it.
